428.title: What the Lord requires (Micah 6:8)
428.hook: to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God
428.howItsDone: On Good Friday the Church chants the Reproaches, built on Micah 6:3, during the veneration of the cross, and Micah 6:8 is quoted in Catholic teaching on justice and mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice like a torrent: Amos the herdsman at the royal shrine, and no songs without justice for the poor. Your line was justice, like a torrent. What just act did you pair with your prayer? Day four hundred twenty-eight.

Micah, called the Morasthite after his home town, preached in the days of the same kings as Isaiah, and in chapter six he stages a trial. God takes his people to court, and calls the mountains and the foundations of the earth as the jury. Then God speaks first, and it isn't an accusation. It's a question: my people, what have I done to thee? How have I been a burden to you? Answer me. Catholics who have been to Good Friday may know that line. It's the heart of the Reproaches, chanted while the cross is venerated, in Latin popule meus, quid feci tibi. A God on trial, asking what he did wrong.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINS AS THE JURY.` → `MY PEOPLE, WHAT HAVE I DONE TO THEE?` → `HEARD AGAIN ON GOOD FRIDAY.`

segments.voice: The people answer, and you can feel them getting nervous. What should I bring? Burnt offerings? Calves a year old? Would God be pleased with thousands of rams, with many thousands of fat goats, or, as the Hebrew has it, rivers of oil? Should I give my firstborn for my sin? Each offer is bigger than the last, until it becomes unthinkable. And then the prophet cuts through it, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will shew thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily, to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God." O man. In Hebrew, adam: any human being, not just one nation. And three things, none of them expensive. Do judgment: act justly, the word Amos used yesterday. Love mercy: the Hebrew word is chesed, the steady loyal love we met in Ruth. Not just do merciful things now and then, but love it. And the third is the strangest. The Hebrew is hatznea lechet, and the first word is unusual and hard to pin down; translators reach for modestly, carefully, attentively. The Latin made it solicitous, so the Douay says walk solicitous: careful, attentive, the way you walk beside someone you don't want to lose. The King James says walk humbly, the way the line is often quoted. Both are trying to catch one hard word. Notice the verb, too: walk. Not arrive. Not achieve. A walk is daily, one step after another, and it's done with someone. The people offered rivers of oil. God asked for a way of walking.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF RAMS, RIVERS OF OIL?` · `O MAN: ADAM, ANY HUMAN BEING.` · `JUSTICE, CHESED, AND A CAREFUL WALK.` · `SOLICITOUS OR HUMBLY: ONE HARD WORD.` · then, large: `WHAT THE LORD REQUIRETH OF THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one of the three for today. Settle, and breathe. Say them over slowly in your head: do justly. Love mercy. Walk humbly. Notice which one tugs at you. Maybe there's something unfair you could set right. Maybe there's someone you could be kind to, steadily, not just once. Maybe you've been walking a little too loud, too sure, and need to walk carefully beside God and other people. Don't pick all three. Pick one, and picture the moment today when you'll do it. If you pray, you can offer that one step to God. The bell holds the time.
What the Lord requires. Micah's answer to a people offering rivers of oil: do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God. Today's word.
Your line: walk humbly. Today, take one walk, even five minutes, and let it be the careful kind, with God beside you. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

options: thousands of rams and ten thousand rivers of oil.
nothing; you argue your case.

fork.reveal: Micah cuts through the bidding war: I will shew thee, O man, what is good. three things, none of them expensive.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice verse for a poster.
what it means: the answer to a people trying to buy God's favor: not rivers of oil, but justice, loyal love, and a careful daily walk.
what a scholar hears: adam, any human; chesed, loyal love; and hatznea, an unusual word, translated solicitous in the Latin and humbly in English.

429.title: Jonah runs (Jonah 1–2)
429.hook: told to go east, he sails west, and prays from inside the fish
429.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Jonah at Mass, especially in Lent, and the Church reads Jonah's three days in the fish as a sign of Christ's three days in the tomb, as Jesus does in the Gospels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Micah's courtroom: not rivers of oil, but justice, mercy, and a careful walk. Your line was walk humbly. Which of the three did you pick? Day four hundred twenty-nine.

The word of the Lord came to Jonas, son of Amathi: arise, go to Ninive, the great city, and preach in it. Ninive, Nineveh, was a great city of the Assyrians, and it lay far to the east, overland. So Jonah gets up. And he goes down to the port of Joppe, on the coast, finds a ship sailing for Tharsis, far off across the sea to the west, pays the fare, and climbs aboard. The text says he was fleeing from the face of the Lord. East was the job. He bought a ticket west.
screen: `ARISE, GO TO NINIVE.` → `NINIVE IS EAST.` → `HE BUYS A TICKET WEST.`

segments.voice: Read it slowly and you notice one verb keeps repeating. Jonah went down to Joppe. He went down into the ship. He went down into the inner part of the ship and fell fast asleep. Down, down, down. Then a great storm. The sailors are terrified; each one cries to his own god and they throw the cargo overboard. And the captain finds the runaway prophet asleep in the hold and has to wake him: get up, call upon thy God. They cast lots to find out whose fault this is, and the lot falls on Jonah. He tells them the truth: I'm a Hebrew, I fear the God who made the sea and the dry land, and I'm running from him. Throw me in, he says, and the sea will calm. And then a detail that's easy to skip: the sailors don't want to. They row hard for land first. Only when they can't make it do they throw him in, and the sea goes quiet, and those sailors end up fearing the Lord and making vows. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now the Lord prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonas: and Jonas was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights." A great fish. The Hebrew says dag gadol; there's no whale in the book of Jonah. And from inside it Jonah prays, the only place he's prayed so far. He went down, he says, to the roots of the mountains, and God brought his life up from corruption. Down was as far as he could go. Jesus pointed to this story as a sign: Jonah three days in the fish, the Son of man three days in the heart of the earth.
screen: `WENT DOWN, DOWN, DOWN.` · `THE SAILORS ROW FOR LAND FIRST.` · `A GREAT FISH, NOT A WHALE.` · `HE PRAYS FROM THE BOTTOM.` · then, large: `THREE DAYS AND THREE NIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name where you're running. Settle, and breathe. Maybe you have a Nineveh too, the thing in the other direction from where you keep buying tickets. A conversation you've avoided for months. An apology. A call to a parent. A decision you keep sleeping through, like Jonah in the hold. Let it come up. Don't fix it, and don't scold yourself. Just name it, quietly, the way Jonah finally told the sailors the truth. If you pray, you can pray from wherever you are right now, even if it feels like the bottom. The bell holds the time.
Jonah runs. The prophet sent east to Nineveh who sails west instead, goes down and down, and finally prays from inside a great fish. Today's word.
Your line: you can't outrun him. Today, take one step toward the thing you named, even if it's only writing it down. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

options: let him sleep; one less person panicking.
wake him and tell him to call upon his God.
throw him overboard right away.
fork.reveal: the captain wakes Jonah: get up, call upon thy God. the pagan sailors pray before the prophet does.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man swallowed by a whale.
what it means: a prophet running from God goes down and down, until from the very bottom he finally prays.
what a scholar hears: the verb yarad, went down, repeats as he flees: to Joppe, into the ship, into the hold, to the roots of the mountains.

430.title: Jonah sulks (Jonah 3–4)
430.hook: the enemy city repents and Jonah is furious that God is merciful
430.howItsDone: Catholics hear Nineveh's repentance read at Mass in Lent, and the Church holds up the Ninevites' fasting and sackcloth as a picture of the penance of the Lenten season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah ran west, went down and down, and prayed from inside the great fish. Your line was you can't outrun him. What step did you take toward your Nineveh? Day four hundred thirty.

The fish puts Jonah out on dry land, and the word of the Lord comes to him a second time, exactly the same: arise, go to Ninive. This time he goes. Ninive is enormous, a three days' walk across, the text says. Jonah walks one day in and preaches a sermon of one sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "Yet forty days, and Ninive shall be destroyed." That's all of it. No call to repent. No promise. No mention of mercy. And the city whose wickedness, God said, had come up before him, believes him.
screen: `THE SAME WORD, A SECOND TIME.` → `A SERMON OF ONE SENTENCE.` → `THE CITY BELIEVES.`

segments.voice: The people proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The news reaches the king, and he gets up from his throne, takes off his robe, and sits in ashes. He decrees that nobody eat, not even the oxen and the sheep; the animals wear sackcloth too. Who knows, he says, whether God will turn and forgive. And God sees what they did, how they turned from their evil way, and doesn't bring the destruction. A prophet's warning, heard at once, from the king down to the cattle. And Jonah is furious. Then he admits why he ran in the first place. I knew it, he says. I knew you are a gracious and merciful God, patient, rich in compassion, ready to forgive. Those are God's own words about himself from Exodus, and Jonah throws them back like a complaint. He'd rather die. God asks one quiet question: do you think you have reason to be angry? Jonah goes out east of the city to watch, hoping. God makes a plant grow over him for shade, and Jonah is very glad of it. Nobody knows what plant it was. The King James says a gourd; Jerome's Latin, and so the Douay, says ivy. When Jerome's new translation reached a church in North Africa, Augustine reported that the congregation nearly rioted over the change. Then a worm kills the plant, a scorching wind blows, and Jonah wants to die again. And God says: you grieve over a plant you didn't plant or grow. Should I not spare Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, and many beasts? And the book ends. On the question. Jonah never answers.
screen: `EVEN THE OXEN WEAR SACKCLOTH.` · `I KNEW YOU WERE MERCIFUL.` · `A GOURD, OR IVY? NOBODY KNOWS.` · `THE BOOK ENDS ON A QUESTION.` · then, large: `SHOULD I NOT SPARE NINEVEH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be glad at someone's second chance. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who got a second chance you're not sure they deserved. A sibling who always gets forgiven. A colleague who messed up and got promoted anyway. A public figure who apologized. Notice the sulk, if there is one, the little part of you sitting east of the city, hoping for fire. Don't scold it. Just let God's question sit next to it: should I not spare them? Then see if you can be glad, even a little. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Jonah sulks. The prophet whose one-sentence sermon saved an enemy city, and who sat outside it, angry that God was merciful. Today's word.
Your line: should I not spare them. Today, when someone gets a second chance, say something kind about it, out loud, to someone. Day four hundred thirty.

options: throw a party with the Ninevites.
get angry, and sit outside the city hoping it burns anyway.
go home quietly to Israel.
fork.reveal: he's furious, and says why he ran: he knew God was gracious and merciful. he sits east of the city to watch.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jonah's story ends when the fish spits him out.
what it means: the second half is the harder story: a prophet angry that God forgave his enemies, and God asking him to care.
what a scholar hears: Jonah quotes God's self-description from Exodus 34:6 as a complaint; and the book ends on an unanswered question, aimed at the reader.

431.title: Job loses everything (Job 1–2)
431.hook: a good man loses children, wealth and health; his friends first sit silent seven days
431.howItsDone: The Church's traditional Office of the Dead draws its readings from Job, and at Catholic wakes visitors come to keep company with the grieving family as much as to speak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah sat east of Nineveh, angry at mercy, and God asked: should I not spare them? Whose second chance were you glad about? Day four hundred thirty-one.

The book opens like a folk tale, in the Douay-Rheims: "There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job." Simple and upright, fearing God. Seven sons, three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, the greatest man in the East. Then the scene shifts to heaven, where the sons of God come before the Lord, and among them is Satan; the Hebrew says ha-satan, the adversary, with the article, like a title in the court. God points out Job. The adversary shrugs: does Job fear God for nothing? Take it all away and see.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF HUS.` → `THE ADVERSARY IN THE COURT.` → `DOES JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOTHING?`

segments.voice: Then the messengers start arriving, each one still speaking when the next runs in. Raiders took the oxen. Fire fell and burned the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And the last: a great wind struck the house where your children were eating, and it fell on them, and they are dead. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and worships: naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked I shall return. The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. Then his health goes too, sores from his feet to his head, and he sits on a dunghill scraping himself with a broken piece of pottery. That's when three friends hear of it, Eliphaz, Baldad and Sophar, and they agree to come together to comfort him. From far off they don't recognize him. They weep aloud, tear their robes, throw dust over their heads. And then the Douay says: "they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no man spoke to him a word: for they saw that his grief was very great." Seven days. No speeches. Nobody explained anything. Hold on to that, because in chapter three Job finally speaks, and then the friends start answering, and for chapter after chapter they explain his suffering to him: he must have done something. At the very end, God says they did not speak rightly about him. Which means the part Job's friends got right was the first week, on the ground, with their mouths shut. The silence came before any of the words.
screen: `MESSENGER AFTER MESSENGER.` · `THE LORD GAVE, THE LORD HATH TAKEN.` · `SEVEN DAYS ON THE GROUND, NO WORD.` · `THEN THEY STARTED EXPLAINING.` · then, large: `THEY SAW THAT HIS GRIEF WAS VERY GREAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice sitting silently with someone in pain. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is suffering right now, if someone comes to mind, someone whose grief is very great. Picture yourself arriving, and sitting down on the ground beside them. Notice the urge to say something: a reason, a bright side, a story about your own aunt. Let the urge pass, and stay. Just be there. That's all the friends did, and it was the part they got right. If you pray, you can hold that person before God without words. The bell holds the time.
Job loses everything. A good man stripped of his children, his wealth and his health, and three friends who sat with him seven days without a word. Today's word.
Your line: they sat with him. Today, be with someone who's hurting, in person or by message, and don't explain anything. Day four hundred thirty-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: the patience of Job, a man who never complained.
what it means: a good man loses everything, and his friends' best comfort is a week of silence; when they start explaining, they go wrong.
what a scholar hears: ha-satan with the article, a courtroom role; the prose frame of chapters 1–2 and 42 wraps long poems of argument.

432.title: Where wast thou (Job 38–42)
432.hook: God answers from the whirlwind with the stars, the sea and the wild ass
432.howItsDone: Catholics hear God's speech from the whirlwind at Sunday Mass in one year of the cycle, paired with the Gospel of Jesus calming the storm, and the Book of Job is read at weekday Mass for a week in autumn of one year of the weekday cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job lost everything, and three friends came and sat on the ground beside him for seven days. Your line was they sat with him. Who did you keep company with? Day four hundred thirty-two.

Thirty-five chapters of argument. The friends say Job must have sinned. Job says he hasn't, and he wants a hearing. He wants God to show up and answer the charge, like a man taking his case to court. Let the Almighty answer me, he says, near the end of his speeches. And then the long poem stops, and the Douay-Rheims says: "Then the Lord answered Job out of a whirlwind." God shows up. Out of a storm. And everyone reading for the first time leans in, because now, surely, we'll find out why.
screen: `THIRTY-FIVE CHAPTERS OF ARGUMENT.` → `LET THE ALMIGHTY ANSWER ME.` → `GOD SPEAKS OUT OF A STORM.`

segments.voice: We don't find out why. God answers Job's questions with questions of his own, and the first one is the title of today: "Where wast thou" when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you understand. Who set its measures? Who shut up the sea behind doors when it burst out of the womb, and said: this far, and no farther? Have you ever commanded the morning? Have you walked in the depths of the sea, or seen the storehouses of the snow? Can you join together the shining Pleiades, or stop Arcturus turning? Who feeds the young ravens when they cry? Who set the wild ass free, to laugh at the noise of the city? It goes on for four chapters: the ostrich, the war horse, the hawk, and two huge creatures, Behemoth and Leviathan. Here's what's strange. God never mentions the wager from chapter one. Never says why Job suffered. Instead he walks Job through a world far bigger and wilder than Job's question, and most of it has nothing to do with people at all. And Job is answered. Not with an explanation, but with a presence. He says, roughly: I had heard of you with my ears, but now my eye sees you. Then two surprises. God tells the friends they did not speak rightly about him, as Job did; Job, who had argued and complained. And Job's fortunes are restored, and he gives his three daughters an inheritance alongside their brothers, which was rare. The Hebrew names them Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch. Jerome translated the names into Latin, so the Douay calls them Dies, Cassia and Cornustibii: Day, Cinnamon, and a horn of eye paint.
screen: `QUESTIONS ANSWERED WITH QUESTIONS.` · `THE PLEIADES, THE RAVENS, THE WILD ASS.` · `NO EXPLANATION, BUT A PRESENCE.` · `NOW MY EYE SEES THEE.` · then, large: `WHERE WAST THOU?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go outside and feel small. If you can, step outside now, or stand at a window. Look up. Clouds, sky, a tree, the light. Let your eyes go as far as they can. Settle, and breathe. Then let one question you carry come to mind, a why that hasn't been answered. Don't push it away. Just hold it up against the size of what you're looking at. The ravens are being fed somewhere right now. Snow is stored up somewhere. If you pray, you can simply be in God's presence, as Job was, without an answer. The bell holds the time.
Where wast thou. God's first question to Job from the whirlwind, opening a tour of creation instead of an explanation. Today's word.
Your line: the whirlwind answered. Today, spend five minutes outdoors looking at something you didn't make and can't control. Day four hundred thirty-two.

433.title: A time for everything (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
433.hook: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to weep and to laugh
433.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 3 is among the Old Testament readings Catholic families may choose for a funeral, and it is also read at weekday Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, God spoke to Job out of the storm, with stars and ravens and the wild ass, and no explanation. Your line was the whirlwind answered. What did you look at outdoors? Day four hundred thirty-three.

Vanity of vanities, the book begins, and all is vanity. The writer gives himself a title, Qoheleth in Hebrew, and in the first two chapters he tries everything: building, gardens, pleasure, wealth, wisdom. Each time he comes back to the same word, hevel, a breath, a vapor, smoke that's gone when you reach for it. The Douay renders it vanity. Then, in chapter three, he stops arguing and writes a list. A folk song once borrowed most of its lines, but they were here first. It's a whole life, two lines at a time.
screen: `VANITY OF VANITIES.` → `HE TRIES EVERYTHING.` → `THEN, IN CHAPTER THREE, A LIST.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven." Then fourteen pairs, each one a time to do something and a time to do its opposite. A time to be born and a time to die. A time to plant and a time to pull up. A time to weep and a time to laugh. A time to mourn and a time to dance. A time to embrace and a time to keep away from embraces. A time to keep silence and a time to speak. A time of war and a time of peace. Twenty-eight times, a whole life in pairs. Notice it's not a to-do list. Nobody chooses a time to die, or a time of war. It's a description: life comes in seasons, and you are always standing in one of them. The Hebrew word for time, et, means the right moment, the fitting time. So the list isn't saying everything happens; it's saying everything has its moment. A few verses later the writer says God has made all things good in their time, and has handed the world over to human minds to ponder; the Hebrew can also be read as eternity set in the heart. And yet nobody can find out the whole work of God from beginning to end. We feel the bigger shape; we only ever see our own season of it. And who is the writer? The Hebrew calls him Qoheleth, a puzzling name that seems to mean one who gathers an assembly. The Greek translated that as Ecclesiastes, from ekklesia, assembly, the same word that later meant church. It is one of the readings a family may choose for a Catholic funeral. It doesn't rush grief. It just says: this, too, has its time.
screen: `ALL THINGS HAVE THEIR SEASON.` · `FOURTEEN PAIRS, TWENTY-EIGHT TIMES.` · `NOT A TO-DO LIST: A DESCRIPTION.` · `QOHELETH, ONE WHO GATHERS.` · then, large: `A TIME TO WEEP, AND A TIME TO LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the season you're in. Settle, and breathe. Go through a few of the pairs slowly and see which one fits right now. Is this a time to plant or a time to pull up? A time to keep silence or a time to speak? A time to embrace, or to keep a little distance? A time to mourn, or, maybe, a time to dance? You might be in more than one. Don't judge the season. Just name it, the way you'd say it's autumn. If you pray, you can offer God the season you're in, and ask to live it well. The bell holds the time.
A time for everything. Ecclesiastes' list of fourteen pairs, from birth and death to war and peace: every season of a life has its moment under heaven. Today's word.
Your line: a time for every purpose. Today, when something feels out of season, say to yourself which time this is, and let it be that. Day four hundred thirty-three.

original.note: Hebrew: time, the fitting moment. it's the word that repeats through every line of the list.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty poem for a sympathy card.
what it means: an ancient list of fourteen pairs saying every part of a life, joy and grief alike, has its season under heaven.
what a scholar hears: et, the fitting time; Qoheleth, the gatherer, rendered Ecclesiastes from ekklesia; and 3:11's olam, world or eternity, set in the human heart.

434.title: Wisdom for every day (Proverbs 9:10; Sirach 6:14)
434.hook: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; a faithful friend is a strong defense
434.howItsDone: Catholics hear Proverbs and Sirach in the Mass readings, especially on weekdays, and the Church counts fear of the Lord among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit received in confirmation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ecclesiastes' fourteen pairs: a time to weep and a time to laugh. Your line was a time for every purpose. Which season did you name? Day four hundred thirty-four, the end of the week.

Proverbs chapter nine sets up two dinner invitations. The first comes from Wisdom, pictured as a woman. In the Douay-Rheims: "Wisdom hath built herself a house, she hath hewn her out seven pillars." She's slaughtered the meat, mixed the wine, set the table, and sent her maids to call from the tower and the walls of the city: whoever is a little one, come in here. Across town, another woman, called Folly, sits at her own door and calls out to the same people walking by, almost word for word. Same street. Same passersby. Two open doors.
screen: `TWO DINNER INVITATIONS.` → `A HOUSE OF SEVEN PILLARS.` → `FOLLY CALLS THE SAME PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Between the two invitations is the line the whole book of Proverbs leans on: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Fear here isn't terror. It's closer to awe, the reverence that knows God is God and I'm not. Catholics count fear of the Lord among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, from the Isaiah passage we read a couple of weeks ago. Wisdom starts there, and then it gets very practical. Which brings us to a second wisdom book, one that's in Catholic Bibles: Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus, not to be confused with yesterday's Ecclesiastes. Its writer signs it near the end: Jesus son of Sirach, of Jerusalem. And a prologue explains that his grandson carried it into Greek in Egypt, with an apology: things said in Hebrew, he says, lose some of their force in another language. In chapter six he talks about friends with real street sense. Some friends are friends for their own convenience, he says, and won't stay in the day of your trouble. Some sit at your table and vanish when things go bad. Test a friend before you trust him. And then: "A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found him, hath found a treasure." Nothing can be weighed against a faithful friend, he adds; such a friend is medicine for life. Look back at this week: Micah's careful walk, Jonah running and sulking, Job's friends sitting silent, the whirlwind, the seasons, and now wisdom in a friend. A week of learning how to live with God and with each other.
screen: `FEAR OF THE LORD: AWE, NOT TERROR.` · `SIRACH, NOT ECCLESIASTES.` · `FRIENDS WHO VANISH IN TROUBLE.` · `NOTHING WEIGHS AGAINST A FRIEND.` · then, large: `HE HATH FOUND A TREASURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a faithful friend. Settle, and breathe. Think of a friend who stayed in the day of your trouble, if one comes to mind. Not the one who was fun at the table, though you might love them too; the one who was there when it went bad. Picture their face. Remember one specific thing they did: a phone call, a ride, a long silence beside you, a hard truth told kindly. Let gratitude come. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. Then decide how you'll tell them today, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Wisdom for every day. Proverbs' beginning, the fear of the Lord, and Sirach's practical wisdom: a faithful friend is a strong defense and a treasure. Today's word.
Your line: a friend is treasure. Today, send that faithful friend a message that says thank you, and name the thing they did. Day four hundred thirty-four.

match.prompt: two wisdom books — tap the pairs.
pairs: Sirach, by Jesus son of Sirach

myth: Ecclesiasticus and Ecclesiastes are the same book
Ecclesiastes is Qoheleth; Ecclesiasticus is Sirach, written by Jesus son of Sirach.
the fear of the Lord in Proverbs means being terrified of God
it's closer to awe and reverence, and Catholics count it among the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
Sirach says to test a friend before you trust him
try him before thou takest him, he says; some friends are companions at the table and won't abide in the day of distress.

fork.setup: you're walking through town. Wisdom calls from her house of seven pillars: come in. a few doors down, Folly calls you with almost the same words. what do you do?
options: go wherever the louder voice is.
go in to Wisdom's table.
keep walking and eat alone.
fork.reveal: both invitations sound alike; Proverbs says the difference begins with the fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom.

original.note: Hebrew: fear, awe, reverence, as in the fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom.

trapdoor: what you thought: proverbs are fortune-cookie sayings.
what it means: wisdom starts in awe of God and turns very practical, down to which friends will stay when things go bad.
what a scholar hears: Ecclesiasticus is Sirach, not Ecclesiastes; and its prologue, where the grandson who carried it into Greek apologizes that Hebrew loses force in translation.
